Hey guys and girls, I recently came into possession of a Commodore 64, and i have absolutely no programming experience. My question to you is: Do you think it is viable to learn programming basics on the C64, then transfer that knowledge to another programming language. Thanks!

Commodore 64 was simpler back then so learning the language is easy, and waaaaay slower. I would go for it.

Transferring knowledge is what makes you a good developer. Not be perfect in syntax in one language but can adapt do the new languages. The most intelligent developers are actually the worst in developing reliable programs.

Also back in the old days, logic mattered. But in nowadays languages logic has long be gone..You are building libraries on top of flawed other libraries. It is more trial and error then designing a perfect system on paper first.

It's BASIC. My first computer was a Commodore 64, and the book that came with it had lots of examples of how to write small programs. If you don't have a disk/tape drive, don't expect to save your work. You could make a weird smiley face that bounced around the screen, change the screen colors,etc.

It can be fun, but I personally don't think you'll find it extremely informative/useful. Get yourself a BASIC interpreter if you are really that interested in learning that language. Otherwise the ROI on your time will be minimal.

My personal biased opinion is that the Commodore 64 is an awesome computer and you should be having with it. There are some BASIC commands without direct equivalents in modern languages (I'm mainly thinking of PEEK and POKE), but I would say most of what you'll learn will be transferable to any language.
You don't really need PEEK and POKE when you have pointers, though.
True, but PEEKing and POKEing doesn't necessarily teach you much about pointers.

What I'm getting at is that if you have pointers, you don't need PEEK and POKE. Similarly, pretty much everything in BASIC without analogues in more modern languages are things that have other, usually better, ways of doing things for whatever language and environment you're using.

Of course you can learn to program on a C64 in BASIC (see sample below) or even better in Assembler. If you do it, you do it to feel how it was 30 years ago. Nowadays it is rather different. I suggest to learn Python as a first language if you don't bother with history or microcontrollers.

10 PRINT "DISCO!!!!!!!"
20 FOR A = 0 TO 15
30 POKE 53280,A
40 POKE 53281,15-A
50 NEXT A
60 GOTO 10
RUN
Oh my, I actually remember POKE 53280+81. I was 11 or 12. Nostalgia!
There's the kid down the road, David Torres, that has a Commodore 64, go ask him. [What I would have said in 1985]
My TI99/4A skills transferred later in life.

I loved the Commodore 64. I learned programming on the Commodore and its contemporaries. I believe that, for its time, the Commodore 64 was the best machine ever made - it stayed relevant for 10 years which is unheard of for a computer.

That said, modern languages are about Object-Oriented programming and there's a big difference between where the Commodore was and where programming is now. I'm trying to learn Swift and there's a lot of stuff I have to unlearn - not so much programming syntax but the way of thinking. It is really, really hard for me to adapt. I'm having a tough time.

Commodore Basic will teach you some 'Basic' things like loops and conditional statements. But as I said, some of what you learn will then need to be unlearned. I don't think it's worth it if you're serious about getting into programming on modern machines. IMO you're probably best off learning a recent version of Visual Basic, or Swift if you're using a Mac.

Actually, thinking about it there is an app development program that is very simple called App Game Kit (AGK). It's a programming language that strongly resembles an older version of Basic. It's unlike a lot of modern languages, too, but it is simple to learn and will be more productive than learning on a Commodore.

There are plenty of modern languages like Python and Lua that don't force objects upon you, and I don't think jumping from BASIC to those languages would require much unlearning at all. You can use them in an object-oriented style, but you don't have to. And then there's functional languages like Haskell that are very different from both BASIC and object-oriented languages.

In general I think you should learn whichever language seems suitable for what you want to do, but there's no harm in learning BASIC as an introduction to the basics (no pun intended), or just for fun.

Variable assignment, loops, basic input / output ideas, and much more is available on C64. So it will at least help you think more like a programmer. On the other hand writing anything now will feel very foreign.

If you like history and would like to see things in context see if you can get a hold of some computer magazines from the era. They would have entire programs to type into your machine. I remember reading the Micro Adventure kids books https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro_Adventure. They included programs, including some that needed to be debugged, as part of the story.

tl;dr More entertaining than directly useful, but still worthwhile.

Why can't you just learn to program on the computer you're posting this on? A C64 is extremely limited, especially with regards to graphics (it can be done, but lack of built in support makes it a real pain).

If you insist on learning on a C64, I'd recommend the Vice Emulator, so you can use decent text editors on your source code, not to mention that slow programs can run much faster if you let the emulator run flat out. Once you have a working program, you could transfer it (manually typing it in, if necessary) onto the real thing.
Homemade Black Bean and Veggie Burger

Ingredients

  • 1 (16 ounce) can black beans, drained and rinsed
  • 1/2 green bell pepper, cut into 2 inch pieces
  • 1/2 onion, cut into wedges
  • 3 cloves garlic, peeled
  • 1 egg
  • 1 tablespoon chili powder
  • 1 tablespoon cumin
  • 1 teaspoon Thai chili sauce or hot sauce
  • 1/2 cup bread crumbs

Directions

  • If grilling, preheat an outdoor grill for high heat, and lightly oil a sheet of aluminum foil. If baking, preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C), and lightly oil a baking sheet.

  • In a medium bowl, mash black beans with a fork until thick and pasty.

  • In a food processor, finely chop bell pepper, onion, and garlic. Then stir into mashed beans.

  • In a small bowl, stir together egg, chili powder, cumin, and chili sauce.
  • Stir the egg mixture into the mashed beans. Mix in bread crumbs until the mixture is sticky and holds together. Divide mixture into four patties.
  • If grilling, place patties on foil, and grill about 8 minutes on each side. If baking, place patties on baking sheet, and bake about 10 minutes on each side.
